name: Battle of Issus
info: Alexander the Great's Hellenic League army defeated the Achaemenid army of Darius III near the Pinarus river by Issus in southern Anatolia in 333 BCE, and Darius fled, leaving his family and treasury to be captured.

facts.place: South of the ancient city of Issus, near present-day Iskenderun in Turkey, on either side of a small river called the Pinarus; the identity of the river is disputed
facts.sides: The Hellenic League under Alexander the Great, perhaps no more than 40,000 men including allies; the Achaemenid Empire under Darius III, whose army is put at no more than 100,000 by most modern historians, against 250,000 to 600,000 in ancient sources
facts.outcome: The Macedonian and allied troops defeated the Persian forces. Darius fled, and Alexander captured his wife, daughters, mother and treasury.

t: Ancient sources put the Persian army at between 250,000 and 600,000 men, while most modern historians think it was no larger than 100,000 and Hans Delbrück gives as few as 25,000.
The battle was fought on a coastal plain only 2.6 km wide between the Gulf of Issus and the mountains, where Darius could not use his superiority in numbers.
It was the first time the Persian army had been defeated with the King present, and the battle has been called the beginning of the end of Persian power.
dyk: Where the Persian army was camped, the distance from the Gulf of Issus to the mountains is only 2.6 km, and the exact course of the Pinarus river there has been argued over for more than 80 years.
ev: Alexander crosses into Asia and defeats the Persian satraps at the Battle of the Granicus
Alexander occupies most of Asia Minor, taking coastal settlements such as Miletus and Halicarnassus
Darius marches north around the mountains, captures Issus and cuts Alexander's supply lines
Alexander's army defeats the Persians on the Pinarus and Darius flees
The Spartan king Agis III defeats the Macedonian general Coragus in the Peloponnese
Agis is finally defeated at the Battle of Megalopolis

sections.background:
Alexander set out into Asia in 334 BCE and defeated the local Persian satraps at the Battle of the Granicus. He then occupied most of Asia Minor, with the idea of capturing all coastal settlements so as to negate the power of the vastly superior Persian fleet. He took several important settlements, among them Miletus in 334 BCE and Halicarnassus.

Darius took personal command of his army after the Granicus. While Alexander was in Tarsus, he heard that Darius was massing a great army in Babylon. If Darius reached the Gulf of Issus, he could use the support of the Persian fleet under Pharnabazus, still operating in the Mediterranean, which would ease his supply and possibly let him land troops behind the enemy. Alexander kept his main army at Tarsus but sent Parmenion ahead to occupy the coast around Issus. In November he received reports that the Persian army had advanced into Syria to a town named Sochoi, and he decided to mass his scattered army and advance south from Issus through the Pass of Jonah.

Darius knew that Parmenion held the Pass of Jonah and chose a northern route. The Persians captured Issus without opposition and cut off the hands of all the sick and wounded that Alexander had left behind. Darius had now placed his army behind the Hellenic advance and cut its supply lines, and Alexander was forced to countermarch.
sections.forces:
Some ancient sources, Arrian and Plutarch, who based their accounts on earlier Greek sources, estimated 600,000 Persian soldiers in total, while Diodorus and Justin estimated 400,000 and Curtius Rufus 250,000. Modern historians find Arrian's count highly unlikely, arguing that fielding more than 100,000 soldiers in battle was extremely difficult at the time. Hans Delbrück gives an estimate as small as 25,000, although most, including Engels and Green, put Darius' army at no more than 100,000, including 11,000 cavalry, 10,000 Persian Immortals and 10,000 Greek mercenaries.

The Hellenic army, led by Alexander, may not have exceeded 40,000 men including allies. It may have consisted of about 24,000 heavy infantry (9,000 phalangites, 3,000 hypaspists, and 7,000 allied and 5,000 mercenary Greek hoplites), 13,000 light infantry (peltasts, archers and slingers) and 5,850 cavalry. Alexander led his Companion cavalry on the right flank and set his Thessalian allied cavalry on the left of the phalanx under Parmenion.

Darius formed his line with his heavy cavalry next to the coast on his right, then the Greek mercenary phalanx, which A. M. Devine puts at 12,000. Next to it he spread his Persian infantry, the Cardaces, along the river and into the foothills, where they wrapped round to the other bank and threatened Alexander's right flank. Arrian gives these troops an inflated figure of 20,000. Darius stood in the centre with the Greek mercenaries, his royal cavalry guard and his best infantry.
sections.course:
The Persian cavalry first charged Parmenion and the allied cavalry, crossing the river to open the battle. Things did not go well for the Macedonians at the start. Their centre phalanx, having to advance across a river and up a fortified bank, suffered severely against the Greek mercenaries waiting on the other side. Arrian noted that a hundred and twenty Macedonians 'of note', probably officers, were killed there, and the Macedonians were forced to retreat across the river. On the left flank the Thessalians struggled against the larger mass of Persian heavy horse, charging and retreating again to buy time.

Then the hypaspists, led by Alexander on foot, attacked the Cardaces and punched a hole through the Persian line. The Agrianians drove back a mass of Persian skirmishers menacing Alexander's far right, which secured the flank of the Companions. Alexander then mounted a horse at the head of his Companions and led a direct assault on Darius and his bodyguards, who fled from the battlefield.

Alexander saw that his left flank and centre were in trouble and, letting Darius go, crashed into the rear of the Greek mercenaries, who broke up and began to retreat as well. The Persians saw that their Great King had gone and that the battle was being lost, and they abandoned their positions and fled in full rout. The Hellenic cavalry pursued them for as long as there was light.
sections.aftermath:
As with most ancient battles, significant carnage occurred after the fighting, as the pursuing Greeks slaughtered their crowded, disorganised foe. Arrian notes Ptolemy mentioning that, while pursuing Darius, Alexander and his bodyguards came upon a ravine which they crossed easily on the piled-up bodies of dead Persians.

Darius fled, leaving behind his family and treasury, which Alexander captured. The Hellenes took Darius' wife Stateira I, his daughters Stateira II and Drypetis, and his mother Sisygambis, all of whom had accompanied him on the campaign. Alexander, who later married Stateira II, treated the captured women with great respect. It was the first time the Persian army had been defeated with the King present.

Later, the Spartan king Agis III recruited the Greek mercenary survivors of the battle who had served in the Persian army, a force of 8,000 veterans, and used them in his fight against the Macedonians. In the summer of 331 BCE Agis defeated Coragus, the Macedonian general in command of the Peloponnese and the garrison of Corinth, but he was finally defeated at the Battle of Megalopolis. Agis used the veterans of the Persian army in his fight against the Macedonians, a use of the survivors that followed directly from the defeat.
sections.sources:
Several ancient writers are named for the battle. Arrian and Plutarch based their accounts on earlier Greek sources and gave 600,000 as the Persian total, Diodorus and Justin 400,000 and Curtius Rufus 250,000. Arrian also gives an inflated figure of 20,000 for the Cardaces, and he notes Ptolemy's mention of the ravine of bodies. Callisthenes' accounts of the measurements of the battlefield and of the distances marched by both armies, together with a distance given by Diodorus after the battle, are the evidence on which the site has been argued.

The site itself is disputed. Speculation on the location of the Pinarus has gone on for over 80 years. Older historians believed it to be the Deli Tchai river, but N. G. L. Hammond and A. M. Devine claim that it is actually the Payas River, Devine using his own examination of its course, which he considered would not have changed drastically since antiquity.

The motives of the two kings are also debated. One modern view, based on Curtius, is that Darius was forced to move his camp to terrain that favoured Alexander, who was fighting defensively on the advice of his war council and Parmenion. In another reading Alexander waited at Myriandus to spring a trap on Darius in the narrow crossing of a pass, and Darius instead went north around the mountains, emerging behind Alexander's position and on his supply lines. On that reading Alexander was caught off guard and forced to march to Darius.
sections.legacy:
The battle is called a decisive Hellenic victory that marked the beginning of the end of Persian power. It was the first time the Persian army had been defeated with the King present, and it was the second major battle of Alexander's invasion of the Persian empire and his first encounter with Darius III. Darius, after fleeing, no longer had his family or his treasury, both of which were in Alexander's hands.

Its shape resembles that of Gaugamela two years later, where Parmenion again held the left wing long enough against superior Persian numbers for Alexander to make his cavalry strike against Darius and break the Persian army. The present-day Turkish city of Iskenderun, close to ancient Issus, bears the Turkish equivalent of Alexandria, a city Alexander founded to commemorate his victory.

The battle has been pictured by later artists. The German Renaissance painter and printmaker Albrecht Altdorfer made The Battle of Alexander at Issus in 1529, and Jan Brueghel the Elder painted The Battle of Issus in about 1599 to 1600; it hangs in the Louvre. Both works are dated well over a thousand years after the battle.

summary: At Issus on 5 November 333 BCE Alexander the Great's army defeated the Persian army of Darius III on a narrow coastal plain in southern Anatolia. Darius fled, and Alexander captured his family and treasury. Ancient and modern figures for the Persian army differ widely.
notes: The source is short and gives no casualty figures for either side and no ancient account of the course by name besides Arrian's remarks on losses and the ravine.
The 'Motives' section is confusingly attributed: the article first says Alexander fought defensively (Curtius-based) then that Darius flanked him. I gave both and did not choose.
The article says the first view is that Darius moved to terrain that favoured Alexander; the second paragraph says Darius caught Alexander off guard. These are presented as competing readings.
The sources section rests on a thin article; some statements there are inferences from named authors in the Combatants, Location and Battle sections, not a source survey the article gives.
The article's text says 'In November Alexander received reports' while the battle is on 5 November; kept as written.
Left out: the Pillar of Jonah passage detail beyond the advance, P. Stratikis's view that Darius copied the Granicus formation, and the Greek names of individual units.
